questions.prompt: A visitor writes one line in the guest book of a school in Sousse: "The pupils looked very smart in their new uniforms." What is she saying about them?

options.text: That they were clever, and answered all her questions.
That they were neat, and dressed with care.
That they were quick, and ran when the bell rang.
That they were polite, and stood up when she came in.

questions.explanation: "That they were neat, and dressed with care." is the meaning: in this lesson smart describes how a person looks, and the line is about the pupils in their uniforms, that is, about their clothes. "That they were clever, and answered all her questions." borrows the meaning that smart carries in American English, where it does mean clever; your book never uses it that way, and a clever pupil in this lesson is called bright or intelligent. "That they were quick, and ran when the bell rang." confuses smart with a word that names speed, which it does not: nothing in the sentence is about moving fast. And "That they were polite, and stood up when she came in." is about behaviour, but a uniform cannot make anybody polite, and the sentence says in their new uniforms, which points straight at appearance.

questions.prompt: Emna is telling two friends how she learns a vocabulary list. Complete what she says: "Cover the right-hand column, and then test ___ on the twelve words, one after the other."

options.text: yourself
themselves
ourselves
yourselves

questions.explanation: "yourselves" is right: Emna is speaking to two friends at once, so you here stands for more than one person, and the plural reflexive ends in -selves. "yourself" is the same pronoun in the singular, for one person only; it is the commonest mistake with this word, because English writes you for one and for many and only the reflexive shows the difference. "themselves" would send the sentence to a third group who are not being spoken to, while Emna is giving her method to the two friends in front of her. And "ourselves" cannot follow an order like cover and test, since an order is always addressed to you and never to we; it would slip Emna herself into an instruction she is giving to somebody else.

questions.prompt: A note is pinned above the shelves of the school library in El Kef: "Every book you take out is recorded at the desk by the librarian." Which sentence says the same thing to a pupil leaving with a book?

options.text: You needn't write your name in the register.
You mustn't write your name in the register.
You had better not write your name in the register.
You ought not to write your name in the register.

questions.explanation: "You needn't write your name in the register." is the sentence: needn't says that an action is not necessary, and the note gives exactly that reason, since the librarian records every book already. "You mustn't write your name in the register." forbids the action, and the note forbids nothing at all; it simply spares you a gesture. "You had better not write your name in the register." is a warning, and a warning announces something unpleasant if you disobey; the note announces nothing of the kind. And "You ought not to write your name in the register." turns the notice into a duty, as if signing the book out were wrong; it is not wrong, it is only pointless.

questions.prompt: Wassim and Nizar revised together every evening before the exams: whenever one of them lost heart, the other found something encouraging to say to him. Which sentence reports exactly that?

options.text: Wassim and Nizar encouraged themselves every evening.
Wassim and Nizar encouraged them every evening.
Wassim and Nizar encouraged each other every evening.
Wassim and Nizar encouraged theirselves every evening.

questions.explanation: "Wassim and Nizar encouraged each other every evening." is right: each other says that the action crosses between two people, the first encouraging the second and the second encouraging the first, which is precisely what the situation describes. "Wassim and Nizar encouraged themselves every evening." says that each boy encouraged himself, two separate actions with nothing passing between them, so the help they gave each other disappears from the sentence. "Wassim and Nizar encouraged them every evening." sends the encouragement to a third group who are not named anywhere; an object pronoun always points away from the subject. And "Wassim and Nizar encouraged theirselves every evening." uses a word that does not exist in English: the reflexive built on they is themselves, and there is no form theirselves.

questions.prompt: Hedi tells his classmates that he spent forty minutes on the first question of Saturday's paper and had to leave the last two blank. Rania wants to tell him, now that it is all over, that this was the wrong thing to do. Which sentence does she use?

options.text: You shouldn't spend forty minutes on a single question.
You shouldn't have spent forty minutes on the first question.
You had better not spend forty minutes on one question in the next paper.
You needn't spend forty minutes on a question worth four marks.

questions.explanation: "You shouldn't have spent forty minutes on the first question." is the sentence: shouldn't have plus the past participle points at an action that has already been done and says it was the wrong one, which is the reproach Rania wants to make about a paper that is over. "You shouldn't spend forty minutes on a single question." is a present modal, so it advises about the papers still to come and lets Saturday pass without a word. "You had better not spend forty minutes on one question in the next paper." names the next paper itself and warns Hedi about the future, when Rania is speaking about the past. And "You needn't spend forty minutes on a question worth four marks." says only that the effort was not necessary, which is not the same judgement: Rania is not telling him he did more than he had to, she is telling him it cost him the two answers he never wrote.
